en: He whose cave of wisdom is profound, whose rock is steadfast mindfulness, who shines with the element of noble speech, from whom flows the spring of loving-kindness, who possesses the power of meditative concentration, and whose mountain cleft is fewness of desires—
he who on this earth was not shaken by the eight haughty winds of worldly dharmas.
I bow to that Perfectly Awakened One, the Sumeru mountain, whose qualities are powerful and whose lofty peaks are wisdom.
He who blazes forth, having overcome all the tenets of rival disputants in the world,
from whose power the bull-like heretics flee in terror;
he who in an instant reduces to ashes even the swarm of moths that are the various [wrong] views.
I bow to that fire of the True Dharma, which utterly consumes the fuel of all latent tendencies.
He who is a thousand-fold crocodile and sea-monster of those in training and those beyond training; whose roar is emptiness;
whose single flavor is liberation; a great jewel-mine of well-spoken words; a lake of moral shame;
and who is nourished by the currents of the river of investigating the meaning of reality—[to him I bow].
I pay homage to the stainless ocean at the head of the assembly, bound by the time of the fetters of training. || 10.1.3 ||
The Sugata, the knower of superior and inferior qualities, declared that the gift of material wealth is not as distinguished as that which is most excellent among those who speak.
The Blessed One spoke on the gift of the Dharma.
For the gift of material goods has a limited scope, whereas the gift of the Dharma has an unlimited scope;
for the fruit of material goods belongs to the realm of desire.
And that very [nature] of the Dharma, and what is beyond it. || 10.1.5 ||
That which is indeed given neither for the sake of wealth,
nor for the sake of honor, nor for the sake of fame—
that is declared to be the supreme gift of Dharma.
Anything other than this is the trade of the true Dharma. || 10.1.6 ||
Having understood this supreme distinction,
the gift of the Dharma should be constantly bestowed;
for material wealth, when given away, indeed comes to an end.
The Dharma being spoken here is expanded. || 10.1.7 ||
Having thoroughly pacified the mind here toward the Blessed One, that mass of virtues, as well as toward his Abhidharma, his Son, and the Noble Saṅgha,
listen with joyful hearts, having approached for the sake of those [teachings].
"O you who are complete, [listen to] the meaning well-spoken by the Sugata, the treasury of glory. || 10.1.8 || Thus.

§1 Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, there are these three persons who are of great benefit to another person. Which three?"

§1.1 When a person, having relied upon another person, goes forth from the home to the homeless state out of genuine faith in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya—shaving off hair and beard, donning saffron robes—this is the first person who is of great benefit to that other person. It is not easy for that [first] person to repay that [second] person even throughout their entire life, namely, by means of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick.

§1.2 Furthermore, there is another person who, having relied upon another person and understood that whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation, develops the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; this is the second person who is of great benefit to another person. It is not easy for that person to repay that person even throughout their entire life with the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.

§1.3 Furthermore, there is another person who, having relied upon a certain person, through the destruction of the outflows, realizes for himself in this very life, by his own direct knowledge, the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; having attained them, he declares: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further state of existence beyond this. This is the third person who is of great benefit to another person.
It is not easy for that person to repay that person even throughout their entire life, namely by means of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
For what reason? Because for that person, there is no other person who is more helpful or more beneficial than that person.

§2 Thus spoke the Blessed One; this was said by the Blessed One, and it was also said by the Arhat: "Monks, there are two kinds of giving: the gift of Dharma and the gift of material things. Monks, of these gifts, the gift of material things is merely minor; the gift of Dharma is the foremost of all gifts."
The Blessed One said this; having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“Those individuals who bestow such gifts as food, drink, hard food, soft food, clothing, and bedding.”
They are not worth even a sixteenth part of the noble gift of Dharma. || 1 ||
To that Protector, the Teacher of gods and humans, the unsurpassed Tathāgata who is compassionate toward all beings, [I offer] the gift of Dharma which he bestowed.
The virtuous pay homage to him who has gone beyond existence. || 2 ||

He spoke as follows: "Toward whom should one not practice pride? Toward whom should one be respectful? For whom is honor appropriate? And for whom should there be the worship of the virtuous? (10.3.1)
Likewise, O gentle one, toward one's mother and father, toward an elder brother, O Mānava, and also toward a teacher, a sub-teacher, and others who are regarded as gurus. (10.3.2)
One should not harbor pride toward them, but should instead be full of reverence for them;
honoring them is virtuous, and their worship is the worship of the righteous.
Those for whom both passion and hatred, as well as ignorance, have faded away; having abandoned pride and being free from arrogance—one should pay homage to them with palms joined. 10.3.4
For just as the noble ones, having examined it with their intelligence, condemn stinginess regarding material things,
so too is stinginess toward the True Dharma possessed of infinite faults.
so too is that [conduct] censured here by those who desire their own welfare. || 10.3.5 ||
In former times, during the Dharma-teaching of Kāśyapa, a monk practiced extreme stinginess regarding the True Dharma;
however, in the final age, he [practiced] the gift of the Dharma.
In this manner, he gave [it] for seven days at that time.
Through the gift of Dharma he went to the third heaven;
but due to the fault of stinginess, he remained in the world of men and understood the Dharma only with extreme difficulty.
For that Sarpadāsa was indeed instructed by Jina. || 10.3.7 ||
The Victor has taught that giving is of two kinds: the gift of material goods and likewise the gift of the Dharma.
Indeed, between these two, the gift of the Dharma is superior.
Because it destroys old age, calamity, and disease. || 10.3.8 ||
Since the Jina has declared that the gift of the sublime Dharma is superior to the gift of material wealth,
therefore the wise [should practice] that which destroys the great disease of the afflictions.
The gift of the Dharma should always be bestowed. || 10.3.9 ||
May the torch of Dharma blaze for a long time, even though the Teacher of the World has long since passed into nirvāṇa;
it dispels the darkness of ignorance and illuminates both the even and the uneven. (10.3.10)
May those gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas,
gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and humans who have come here to hear the Dharma protect this world and the teaching of the Jina.
And let them always practice the Dharma taught by the Lord of Sages.
